chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Yunus ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

It was said to him, while I was present: 'The man happens to be in his salat, devoid (of distractions), then self-conceit (ujb) enters him.' So he said: 'When the beginning of his salat was with an intention seeking his Lord, then whatever enters him after that will not harm him. So let him continue in his salat and let him debase Satan.'

key_terms.الْعُجْبُ: Ujb — self-conceit, self-admiration, or spiritual vanity; a blameworthy spiritual state where one becomes pleased with one's own worship, considering it a personal virtue
key_terms.خَالِياً: Free/devoid — in the context of salat, meaning undistracted, fully focused, in a state of khushu' (reverence)
key_terms.نِيَّة: Niyyah — intention; the internal determination that directs an act of worship toward God; the key criterion in Islamic legal thought for the validity of worship

ai.seo_question: Does self-conceit (ujb) during prayer invalidate the salat in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked — in the presence of the narrator Yunus ibn Ammar — about a man who begins his prayer in a state of focus but is later afflicted by ujb (self-conceit or vanity). The Imam ruled that as long as the prayer began with a sincere intention directed toward God, any subsequent spiritual distraction such as ujb does not invalidate the prayer. The worshipper should complete his salat and mentally repel Satan, who is the source of such intrusive thoughts.
